To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the education system in Pakistan, through curriculum and school practice, promotes a gendered, exclusionary, and homogenous concept of citizenship that contributes to identity based violence against women and religious minorities.
The Pakistan Studies textbook and school practices promote an exclusionary, gendered and religiously based concept of citizenship that contributes to identity based violence in Pakistani society.

the Pakistan Studies textbook, the school's curriculum and the teachers' and the students' own understandings of what it means to be a Pakistani citizen are based in an exclusionary and gendered concept of a legitimate Muslim citizen, and that the school simultaneously mitigates and exacerbates other social divisions.

how the education system in Pakistan contributes to identity based violence against women and minority groups.
the ways in which education can reproduce gendered and exclusionist notions of citizenship that contribute to the reproduction of violence in Pakistan.
the question of whether the school is reproducing the social divisions that are present in society.

this case study of a girls' government school shows that education in Pakistan reproducing a gendered and exclusionist notion of citizenship that is rooted in the notion of the ideal Muslim women.

the education system in Pakistan is reproducing a homogeneous concept of the legitimate citizen (male Muslim Sunni) and that it contributes to identity based violence against those that do fit into this conception.

the education system in Pakistan, as represented by this girls' school, is not adequately addressing the social and political issues that contribute to identity based violence against girls and other marginalized groups.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this study shows that the Pakistan Studies textbook and the school's practice reproduce a homogeneous notion of a legitimate citizen that is based in the ideal Muslim man.

the school is reproducing the ideal of a citizen in a way that is both gendered and exclusionist, and that it is doing so by reproducing a gendered understanding of the role of the ideal woman in countering violence.
this research is about the intersection of education, violence and citizenship in a post-colonial state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the education system in Pakistan is a site of contestation, where multiple discourses of citizenship and violence are produced and reproduced.

the education system in Pakistan is a key site for social transformation and that the education system needs to be reformed to include more diverse perspectives and to promote critical pedagogies that promote a more inclusive and equitable concept of citizenship and a vision for a more peaceful and inclusive society.

we must critically examine the ways in which education can be used to reproduce violence, and that we must be careful to not use education as a tool for social change without first critically examining the ways in which the education system itself can be a source of violence.
